name: Dunning-Kruger in QC
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Vocabulary Trap: Confidence Without Competence in Quantum Computing
lesson.summary: Explains why learning a handful of quantum computing terms can make non-experts feel more qualified to judge the field than they actually are, and why this specific bias is especially dangerous around quantum claims.
lesson.body:
You already know that cognitive biases distort judgment in predictable, systematic ways rather than randomly. The Dunning-Kruger effect is one of the more unsettling ones: people with limited knowledge of a subject tend to overestimate how much they actually understand it, precisely because the skills needed to perform well in a domain are often the same skills needed to recognize when you're performing badly. If you don't have those skills yet, you're missing the very tool that would tell you what you're missing. This is not about stupidity ,  it's a structural gap between "knowing some facts" and "knowing how those facts fit into a working model," and quantum computing sits right on top of that gap.

Here's the mechanism in action. Quantum computing has a small set of vivid, quotable terms ,  superposition, entanglement, qubit, decoherence ,  that show up constantly in press coverage and pitch decks. Learning what these words *point to* is genuinely easy: superposition means a qubit can be in a combination of 0 and 1 states rather than strictly one or the other; entanglement means qubits can be correlated in ways that have no classical analogue. That took you one paragraph. But knowing what the words mean is completely different from being able to evaluate whether a specific quantum processor with, say, 100 physical qubits is actually useful for a given problem, whether its error rates permit meaningful computation, or whether a claimed "quantum advantage" result generalizes to anything practically important. That evaluation requires understanding gate fidelities, error correction overhead, decoherence timescales, and how noise compounds across circuit depth ,  none of which is conveyed by the vocabulary alone. The gap between "I can define entanglement" and "I can assess this company's technical roadmap" is enormous, and the bias is that the vocabulary fluency feels like it closes that gap when it doesn't even touch it.

This matters more in quantum computing than in many other technical fields because the field's real complexity is unusually well hidden behind approachable-sounding words. Contrast this with, say, evaluating a new battery chemistry, where the jargon itself signals unfamiliarity and keeps people appropriately cautious. Quantum terms sound almost intuitive ,  "superposition" evokes something like "being in two places at once" ,  which makes people feel they've grasped the concept when they've only grasped a metaphor for it. An investor who can toss around "qubit coherence time" in a meeting may feel entitled to weigh in on whether a company's technology is two years or twenty years from commercial viability, when in fact assessing that timeline requires judgment about hardware engineering, error correction thresholds, and materials science that vocabulary contributes essentially nothing toward.

The practical danger is that this false confidence doesn't stay private ,  it shapes investment decisions, policy funding, and public expectations, and those decisions get made by people who genuinely believe they've done their homework because they can use the right words fluently. Recognizing this bias doesn't mean distrusting every non-physicist's opinion; it means noticing when comfort with terminology is being treated as a substitute for the deeper, harder-won understanding of mechanism that actual technical evaluation requires.
